podcasts.name: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

member_of.name: Scott Wyland and the Action Girls

podcast.title: Heroin Addiction Discovery (1993)
podcast.body: Following the success of Stone Temple Pilots' debut album "Core," it was discovered that Scott Wyland had become a heroin addict while the band was in the midst of selling millions of records. "STP signing their major label record deal, going on tour, and then finding out that their lead singer had become a heroin addict while the band was selling millions of records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: $6 Million Drug Spending (1994-1998)
podcast.body: In May 1998, Scott Wyland candidly revealed that he had spent over $6 million on drugs between 1994 and early 1998. "He spoke candidly of his drug problems, declaring that he had spent over $6 million on drugs between 1994 and early 1998."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Detox Attempt (Spring 1994) – Exodus Recovery Center
podcast.body: In spring 1994, Wyland intended to check into the Exodus Recovery Center in Marina del Rey for detox. He was advised against it because two other "major junkies," Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers (who allegedly introduced Wyland to heroin) and Kurt Cobain, were already present. "There are two major junkies already on the premises and that will not help you kick your habit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lying to His Wife While on Tour (1994)
podcast.body: While on tour and addicted to heroin, Scott frequently called Janina and falsely claimed he was not using drugs. Despite feeling guilty about his deception, he continued his drug use. "He told her he wasn't using, which was a lie of course, and even though he felt bad about lying, he didn't stop using it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marriage to Janina Costenda (September 17, 1994)
podcast.body: Scott Wyland married his longtime girlfriend, Janina Costenda, in a lavish ceremony held in a wealthy area of Pasadena on September 17, 1994. "And on September 17th, 1994, he and his longtime girlfriend, Janina Costenda, were married in a lavish ceremony in a rich area of Pasadena."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Wedding Life (1994)
podcast.body: After their honeymoon, Scott and Janina purchased the house where their wedding took place and began accumulating antiques and cars. "After the honeymoon, Scott and Janina bought that house, the house where they actually had the wedding and began collecting antiques and cars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Repeated Relapses and Rehab Stays (1994-1997)
podcast.body: Between 1994 and 1997, Scott Wyland entered rehabilitation facilities a staggering thirteen times, indicative of his persistent struggles with addiction and repeated relapses. "Between 1994 and 1997, he went to rehab 13 times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rumors of Drug Problem (End of 1994)
podcast.body: By the end of 1994, rumors began to circulate widely regarding Scott Wyland's condition, with many hinting at a significant drug problem and other "dark things." "By the end of 1994, rumors had begun to swirl about Scott's condition."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Wedding Day Drug Use (September 17, 1994)
podcast.body: Prior to his wedding ceremony, Scott Wyland consumed cocaine in the limo with some of his groomsmen. "Scott bit a little coke in the limo with some of his groomsmen before the ceremony, but Emes is wedding day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drug Treatment Agreement (May 1995)
podcast.body: Following his May 1995 drug bust, Wyland was informed by the court that he could avoid a criminal record if he successfully completed a drug treatment program, a condition he agreed to. "Wyland was told that if he completed a drug treatment program, he would be free to go without a criminal record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pasadena Drug Bust (May 15, 1995)
podcast.body: At approximately 3:30 AM on Monday, May 15, 1995, in Pasadena, California, Scott Wyland was apprehended by police after being seen leaving the rear of a CD motel with his lights off. Officers, suspecting a drug transaction, found a chunk of Mexican black tar heroin in his wallet upon apprehension. "When they caught up with Scott, the cops found a chunk of Mexican black tar heroin in Wyland's wallet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Arrest Drug Seeking (May 15, 1995)
podcast.body: Immediately after being released on $10,000 bail (posted by his wife), Scott Wyland demanded that Janina drive him to his dealer's house to "score" drugs. When she refused, he jumped out of their 1965 Mustang while it was moving at 15-20 miles per hour. "When she refused, Scott jumped out of the car while it was still moving at 15 or 20 miles an hour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Public Statement of Remorse (May 1995)
podcast.body: While at the Chateau Marmont, Scott Wyland prepared a tearful statement of remorse which Courtney Love then called a local radio station in the middle of the night to read live on air. In the statement, he apologized to his friends, band, wife, family, and acknowledged becoming a "hypocrite" to social ideals, expressing a desire to recover and create more music. "I have a disease it went. I want to say sorry to my friends, my band, my wife, and my family and to the social ideals to which I have become a hypocrite. I ache to get well, to feel, and to make more music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rehab in Colorado (Summer 1995)
podcast.body: Scott Wyland spent part of the summer of 1995 at a rehabilitation facility located in Colorado, returning to Los Angeles by the end of August that year. "He agreed and spent part of that summer at a rehab facility in Colorado."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Seeking Solace with Courtney Love (May 1995)
podcast.body: After Janina refused to allow him back home following his arrest and subsequent behavior, Scott Wyland sought refuge with Courtney Love, who was staying at the Chateau Marmont Hotel on Sunset Boulevard. "When Jeanine refused to let Scott come home, he sought solace in of all people, Courtney Love, who had a room with the Chateau Marmont Hotel on sunset bullifard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cocaine and Heroin Charges Dropped (October 29, 1996)
podcast.body: A judge dropped all cocaine and heroin charges against Scott Wyland on October 29, 1996, having been satisfied that he had successfully completed the court-prescribed drug treatment program. "On October 29, 1996, a judge dropped all cocaine and heroin charges against Scott."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disappearance Rumors (1996)
podcast.body: Rumors circulated that Wyland had either bolted to Detroit to attend a Kiss concert or sought to investigate whispers that he was about to be replaced as Stone Temple Pilots' lead singer (rumors that eventually proved true). "One dumb rumor was that he had bolted for Detroit so he could attend a kiss concert."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Escape from Rehab (June 26, 1996)
podcast.body: After being transferred to Impact House, a residential drug treatment facility, for what was supposed to be a six-month stay, Scott Wyland disappeared on June 26, 1996. An arrest warrant was issued for him. "But then on June 26th, Wyland disappeared."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Marriage Ends (1996)
podcast.body: His marriage to Janina Costenda ended because she "just couldn't take it anymore" amidst his ongoing drug issues and legal troubles. "And to make matters even worse, his marriage to Janina was over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Probation Violation Arrest (April 23, 1996)
podcast.body: On April 23, 1996, police moved to arrest Scott Wyland for missing one of his mandatory drug counseling sessions. Before officers arrived, friends intervened and sent him to a hospital, from where he was transferred to the medical unit of the LA County Jail. "What actually had happened was that Wyland had missed one of his mandatory drug counseling sessions and police moved in to arrest him on April 23, 1996."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relapse After Tour (December 29, 1996)
podcast.body: After a successful six-week tour with Stone Temple Pilots, Scott Wyland called Dean DeLeo on December 29, 1996, confessing that he had "fallen off the wagon. Hard." "Scott had called Dean Delayo at home on December 29th. He confessed that he had fallen off the wagon. Hard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return to Court (1996)
podcast.body: Before he could be located by the warrant, Scott Wyland reappeared "safe and sober" at the Pasadena Municipal Court, explaining his disappearance as a need to speak with his wife about a personal problem. "Wyland turned up safe and sober at the Pasadena Municipal Court."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Voluntary Rehab Entry (December 30, 1996)
podcast.body: On December 30, 1996, Scott Wyland voluntarily checked into rehab once again, marking his thirteenth time entering such a facility in three years. He vowed at this point that he would get well "once and for all." "But this time, he swore he was going to get well once and for all."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 13 Days on the Run (July 1998)
podcast.body: Scott Wyland was on the run for almost thirteen days, with a continent-wide APB (all-points bulletin) issued for his arrest. His manager and lawyer refused to disclose his whereabouts during this period. "Wylandt was on the land for almost 13 days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arresting Officer's Reaction (June 1, 1998)
podcast.body: The police officer who arrested Scott Wyland in Manhattan was reportedly heartbroken, as he was a huge Stone Temple Pilots fan and had been following Wyland's story in the press. He had not anticipated being the one to send Wyland back to jail. "The arresting officer was heartbroken. He was a huge STP fan, and had been following Wylandt's story in the press."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Court Delays (Late 1998 - Early 1999)
podcast.body: His court case was repeatedly postponed, initially from December 10, 1998, to January 22, 1999, and then again to February 16, 1999, due to ongoing issues on the West Coast. "His court case was then pushed to January 22nd 1999, then February 16th 1999."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disappearance After Bail (July 1998)
podcast.body: After his arrest in New York City, Wyland was released on bail but subsequently disappeared, failing to appear for his scheduled court date on July 31. "As soon as he was out on bail, he was gone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Disappearance from Courthouse (July 9, 1998)
podcast.body: On the morning of Thursday, July 9, 1998, Scott Wyland was last seen smoking cigarettes and answering questions on the steps of the Los Angeles County Courthouse. Upon hearing about the $250,000 arrest warrant, he vanished, knowing he would be arrested if he entered the building. "He knew that he'd be arrested the second he put inside, so he vanished."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dual Coast Legal Troubles (1998)
podcast.body: Following his July 1998 arrest, Scott Wyland faced drug felony charges in both California and New York, necessitating his legal team to coordinate multiple court dates and hearings across the country. "Wylandt was up on drug felony charges in both California and New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extended Rehab Stay (1998)
podcast.body: Wyland remained in rehab for an additional four months, aware that a conviction for his charges could result in up to a year of jail time. "Wylandt stayed in rehab for another four months and the whole time he was there, he knew he faced jail time if convicted up to a year in fact."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hit Parader Magazine Feature (1998)
podcast.body: Hit Parader magazine published a story with the headline "Scott Wyland in full control," highlighting a period where things seemed to be improving for him. "Hit Parader magazine even published a story under the headline, Scott Wylandt in full control."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: LA Drug Purchase Arrest (July 22, 1998)
podcast.body: At 6:30 PM on Tuesday, July 22, 1998, Scott Wyland was arrested at 6th and Burlington Street near downtown Los Angeles for simply buying drugs, rather than on the outstanding arrest warrant. Drugs were found on his person. "The police weren't looking for him because of that arrest warrant. They picked him up because he was simply buying drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manhattan Drug Bust (June 1, 1998)
podcast.body: On Monday, June 1, 1998, two weeks after his solo album's release and the day before a planned New York City gig, Scott Wyland was arrested at 3:00 PM. He was picked up leaving 20 Avenue D on Manhattan's Lower East Side, a building known for housing drug dealers, where police found ten $10 decks of heroin (valued at $100 each). "They found ten decks of heroin, ten dollar packages of smack, that were worth about a hundred dollars a piece."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Missed LA Court Dates (June/July 1998)
podcast.body: Judge Larry Fiddler in Los Angeles, assigned to Wyland's case, required him to appear at court hearings to monitor his sobriety. Wyland missed a June 11 hearing (excused as he was in rehab) and a subsequent early June appearance, prompting Judge Fiddler to issue a $250,000 arrest warrant. "Wylandt missed the first hearing on June 11th, but he had an excuse. He was in a drug rehab facility."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: NYC Court Date Continuance (July 31 to November 4, 1998)
podcast.body: His New York attorney, Robert Kalina (who also represented Biggie Smalls and Run DMC), successfully argued that Wyland was unable to appear for his July 31 court date because he was in rehab in California. Judge Thomas Farber and District Attorney Christine Hatfield agreed to postpone the hearing until November 4, 1998. "Wylandt's New York attorney, Robert Kalina, who worked with rap artists like Biggie Smalls and run DMC, successfully convinced the court that Wylandt was unable to appear because he was in fact in rehab again in California."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New Management and Sobriety Efforts (1998)
podcast.body: A new management company took over Scott Wyland's affairs, ensuring he attended Narcotics Anonymous meetings. Reportedly, he was not consuming anything stronger than coffee at this time. "His new management company was making sure that Wylandt was going to his narcotics anonymous meetings, and as far as anybody could tell, he wasn't taking anything stronger than coffee."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Weight Loss (November 1998)
podcast.body: By November 1998, Wyland weighed 148 pounds, a relatively low weight for someone just under six feet tall. "At the time, Wyland weighed 148 pounds. Not a lot for a guy a shade under six feet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Last Night of Freedom" Performance (August 12, 1999)
podcast.body: Prior to turning himself in for sentencing, Scott Wyland performed what was described as one of Stone Temple Pilots' finest shows in Las Vegas on August 12, 1999. He told his bandmates, "I couldn't think of three other people to spend my last night of freedom with." "I mean, one of the last things he said to us while we were in the room alone was, you know, I couldn't think of three other people to spend my last night of freedom with, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arrest and Jail After Vegas Show (August 13, 1999)
podcast.body: Immediately after the August 12, 1999 Las Vegas concert, Scott Wyland was arrested and sent to jail as per court orders. "After the show, Wyland was arrested and sent to jail."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Divorce Still Pending (End of 1999)
podcast.body: As of the end of 1999, Scott Wyland's divorce from Janina Costenda had still not been finalized. "As of the end of 1999, the divorce still hadn't come through."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Release to Halfway House (December 31, 1999 - January 13, 2000)
podcast.body: Reports in January 2000 indicated Wyland would be released early. He was moved from jail to a halfway house on January 13, 2000, having been out of jail since December 31, 1999. "On January 13th, 2000, fans learned that he had been moved out of jail into a halfway house."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Guilty Plea and Probation (February 16, 1999)
podcast.body: On February 16, 1999, Wyland finally appeared in New York City court for his drug charge and pleaded guilty. In exchange, he received no jail time on the condition that he remain out of trouble for one full year, with any violations resulting in a 30-day sentence at Rikers Island. "That was an exchange for no jail time and on the condition that he stayed at a trouble for one full year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jail Routine (Late 1999)
podcast.body: During his time in jail, Wyland lived in a dormitory, waking at 5:30 AM daily. He attended meetings and drug counseling sessions at 7 AM and 7 PM, had a few hours of free time after supper, and lights were out at 10 PM. He was not permitted to listen to music. "He was not allowed to listen to music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: One-Year Jail Sentence (September 3, 1999)
podcast.body: On Friday, September 3, 1999, Scott Wyland was sentenced to one year in the LA County Jail for a probation violation stemming from August 1998. Judge Fiddler dismissed letters and testimonials from friends and drug counselors presented by Wyland's attorney. "So one year in the LA County jail, Sobs broke out on the courtroom when the verdict was read."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ordered Back to Rehab (June 1999)
podcast.body: A frustrated Judge Fiddler, growing "a little tired of Wyland's face," ordered him into yet another rehabilitation facility after his probation violation. "So he ordered him into another rehab facility."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Probation Violation and Jail (January 15, 1999)
podcast.body: On Friday, January 15, 1999, Scott Wyland was arrested in Los Angeles for a probation violation. This occurred when he voluntarily appeared in court to amend his driver's privileges, and the court discovered he had failed to provide a urine sample to his parole officer to prove sobriety. He was jailed from Friday night until Wednesday morning. "Scott had failed to provide to his parole officer a year in sample to prove that he was still clean."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Probation Violation at Impact House (April 1999)
podcast.body: On June 4, 1999, Judge Fiddler received a report from Impact House stating that Wyland had been dropped from their treatment program on April 16 for non-compliance, either by failing to provide a urinalysis or by submitting a sample that tested positive for drugs. "Wyland had been dropped from treatment on April 16th for failing to comply with the program."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relationship with Mary Forsberg (February 1999)
podcast.body: At his New York court appearance where he pleaded guilty, Scott Wyland was accompanied by Mary Forsberg, a model who was identified as his new girlfriend. "An interesting thing about this court appearance was that he was accompanied by Mary Forsberg, a model, and apparently Wylandt's new girlfriend."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scolding and Return to Rehab (January 1999)
podcast.body: After being released from jail, Judge Fiddler issued a stern reprimand before sending Wyland back to rehab once more. "And after a big scolding from Judge Fiddler, Wylandt was sent back to rehab again, then back to New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Accepting Full Responsibility (March 2000)
podcast.body: Around March 2000, Wyland was described as "fully accepting responsibility for where he is," not complaining or wincing, but completely owning the situation he had created for himself. "He's accepting complete and full responsibility for the web he has woven."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Career (Post-2000)
podcast.body: After 2000, Wyland's career included further Stone Temple Pilots reunions, firings, another solo album, another non-STP band, and his involvement with Velvet Revolver. "There's still an STP reunion or two, a firing or two, another solo album, another non-STP band, and the whole velvet revolver thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Plans to Marry Mary Forsberg (May 2000)
podcast.body: Plans were in place for Scott Wyland and Mary Forsberg to get married in May 2000, despite his divorce from Janina still not being finalized at that time. "There were even plans for Scott and Mary to get married in May, despite, like I said, that Scott's divorce from Janina still hadn't been finalized."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Snowboarding with Mary (February 2000)
podcast.body: In February 2000, Scott Wyland and his girlfriend, Mary Forsberg, were permitted to go snowboarding as part of his supervised release. "In February, he and his girlfriend Mary were allowed to go snowboarding."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1990s Era Voice
podcast.body: Scott Wyland's voice was recognized as one of the great voices of the 1990s, making a significant impact on listeners despite his well-known personal struggles. "If you grew up in the 1990s, his was one of the great voices of that era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Drug-Fueled Recording of Purple (1994)
xref.body: The recording of the "Purple" album in Atlanta was notably swift, completed in just four weeks, largely because Scott Wyland's local dealer, a 25-year-old HIV-positive woman, supplied him with drugs that prevented him from becoming "dope sick," thus enabling continuous work. "Her stuff kept Scott from getting dope sick, which meant that the album was recorded rather quickly, four weeks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exodus Recovery Center Stay (Spring 1994)
xref.body: Gibby Haynes was present at the Exodus Recovery Center in Marina del Rey during spring 1994, at the same time Scott Wyland was considering checking into the facility for detox, leading to Wyland's decision not to check in. "There are two major junkies already on the premises and that will not help you kick your habit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exodus Recovery Center Stay (Spring 1994)
xref.body: Kurt Cobain was a 27-year-old from Seattle who was at the Exodus Recovery Center in Marina del Rey during spring 1994, at the same time Scott Wyland was considering checking into the facility for detox. "The second was a 27 year old guy from Seattle named Kurt Cobain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Rehab Escape and Death (Spring 1994)
xref.body: Just a few days after Scott Wyland considered checking into rehab, Kurt Cobain escaped from the facility, made his way home, and subsequently died by suicide. This event significantly impacted Scott Wyland, exacerbating his own struggles. "And few days Kurt would escape from rehab, make his way home, and then shoot himself. This did not help Scott with his issues."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Side Project Contributions (1995)
xref.body: This side project, formed by Scott Wyland, contributed a song to the "Tank Girl" movie soundtrack, which was curated by Courtney Love, and also to a John Lennon tribute album. "He'd also formed a side project called the Magnificent Bastards, a group that contributed a song to the Tank Girl soundtrack, which by the way was curated by Courtney Love, and also a John Lennon tribute album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Fit and Ready to Rock" Reunion Press Conference (October 1, 1996)
xref.body: At the same location where they announced Scott Wyland's departure, Stone Temple Pilots held a press conference on October 1, 1996, declaring that all members were "fit and ready to rock" after Wyland's drug treatment. Scott expressed the importance of his bandmates, stating, "It's an important thing to me to have these guys in my life. It's a relationship. It's not just about the band and business."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Isolation for Writing Tiny Music (1996)
xref.body: For their third album, the band rented actor Jimmy Stewart's mansion in Santa Barbara, believing the isolation would benefit everyone, particularly Scott Wyland, in their writing process. Despite this, Wyland frequently traveled down the Pacific Coast Highway to Los Angeles to purchase cocaine and heroin. "He was thought that the isolation would do everyone, especially Scott, a lot of good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Public Statement on Tour Cancellation (April 1996)
xref.body: Stone Temple Pilots issued a public statement clarifying the cancellation of their tour dates, explicitly attributing it to Scott Wyland's "dependency on drugs" and his being "under a doctor's care in a medical facility." The statement emphasized that it was not due to typical reasons like exhaustion, dehydration, or a sore throat. "Our lead singer, Scott Wyland has become unable to rehearse or appear for these shows due to his dependency on drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Wyland's Temporary Departure (1996)
xref.body: Scott Wyland was effectively "out" of Stone Temple Pilots after the band suggested he pay millions in restitution for the canceled tour dates, a period that coincided with the end of his marriage to Janina. "And that was it for STP as Scott was concerned. He was out, especially after he was suggested that he pay some kind of restitution for the canceled dates out of his own pocket, which meant millions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Six-Week Road Trip with Guardian (November 4 - December 14, 1996)
xref.body: The band embarked on a six-week road trip beginning November 4 in Los Angeles, concluding in Cleveland on December 14. Scott Wyland was required to be accompanied by a guardian and adhere to a nightly curfew, with a decision made to avoid crossing international borders to minimize potential hassles with customs due to Wyland's history. "Wyland was to be accompanied by a guardian and was required to meet a nightly curfew."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tiny Music Songs from the Vatican Gift Shop (1996) – Third Album

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tour Cancellation Due to Scott Wyland's Addiction (1996-1997)
xref.body: The band was forced to cancel a substantial portion of their tour supporting "Tiny Music" throughout late 1996 and into 1997 due to Scott Wyland's persistent drug issues and his inability to rehearse or perform. The band stated, "Our lead singer is a junkie with the message and we can't go on the road with him until he's well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Trippin' on a Hole in a Paper Heart (1996)

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Impact of Scott's Relapse on Album Charts (January 1997)
xref.body: Scott Wyland's relapse and subsequent undetermined rehab stay came at a time when "Tiny Music" had significantly climbed the album charts, jumping 78 spots in a month due to the recent tour, causing frustration for the other band members. "Tiny music had jumped 78 spots on the album charts in a month because of the tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manager's Statement on Scott's Relapse (January 6, 1997)
xref.body: On January 6, 1997, STP's manager Steve Stewart issued a statement confirming Scott Wyland was having problems again and was seeking care, but assured that he was safe, not arrested, and the band remained together. "Scott has made the band aware that he was having problems again and is taking care of himself at this point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Multiple DUIs and Bizarre Arrest (1998)
xref.body: Scott Weiland had a history marked by numerous DUIs. In a particularly bizarre incident in 1998, he was arrested while attempting to purchase crack cocaine, at the time dressed as a pimp. "Scott Wyland, so many DUIs, and then there was the time in 1998 when he was arrested trying to buy a crack while dressed as a pimple."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Therapeutic for Band Members (1998)
xref.body: The other Stone Temple Pilots members found the process of making the "Talk Show" record to be "therapeutic" for them, much like Scott Wyland found his solo album therapeutic. This experience taught them valuable lessons, particularly about their chemistry and mutual importance. "I think after the talk show thing, I think the talk show record was really therapeutic for all of us to make."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Canceled Gigs Due to Probation Violation (June 1999)
xref.body: A gig scheduled for June 11 in New York City was canceled after Impact House reported Scott Wyland's probation violation, leading to Judge Fiddler ordering him back to rehab. "A gig in New York City, Schedule for June 11th was canceled, and there was a matter of a show set for Las Vegas in August the 12th."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Las Vegas Show Before Incarceration (August 12, 1999)
xref.body: The band performed an acclaimed show in Las Vegas on August 12, 1999, which became Scott Wyland's "last night of freedom" before he had to turn himself in for sentencing. The band described the experience as surreal, witnessing their friend taken away by a bailiff the next morning after a great performance. "We watched our friend be taken away by a 200 pound bailiff, man. It was the most surreal four days you'd ever want to experience."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lollapalooza Headliner Rumors (March 1999)
xref.body: Following positive progress reports on Scott Wyland in March 1999, rumors suggested that Stone Temple Pilots would headline Lollapalooza if the festival were to be reactivated. "There were rumors that if Lola Paloza were to be reactivated, STP would be the headliners."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Reunion and Renewed Chemistry (February 1999)
xref.body: After their separate projects, the other three members realized the importance of their collective "chemistry" and Dean DeLeo called Scott Wyland, who, feeling "out of options," agreed to rejoin. They entered the studio in February 1999 with Brendan O'Brien to work on their fourth album, "Number 4." "One of them was chemistry. We looked at each other in a different way and thought, this is what we mean to each other."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: VH1 Special (March 8, 2000)
xref.body: All four members of Stone Temple Pilots traveled to New York on March 8, 2000, to tape a special for the video channel VH1, marking a public appearance after Scott Wyland's recent release from jail and halfway house. "On March 8th, all four members of the band went to New York where they taped a special for VH1, the video channel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manufactured Supergroup (2004)
xref.body: Velvet Revolver was openly acknowledged as a "manufactured product" assembled by managers, essentially a combination of Guns N' Roses members with Scott Weiland and another musician, rather than a naturally formed group. "It was a manufactured product put together as a supergroup by various managers. It was basically guns and roses with Scott Wyland and some other guy."

xref.title: Firing of Scott Weiland (February 27, 2013)
xref.body: On February 27, 2013, Stone Temple Pilots officially terminated Scott Weiland, issuing a one-line statement. This decision came as the band believed Weiland had reverted to his old ways with drug abuse. This led to "back and forth lawsuits" before settling. "Even temple pilots have announced they have officially terminated Scott Wyland. In other words, they fired him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Departure (2013)
xref.body: In February 2013, Scott Weiland was removed from the band due to excessive drug and alcohol use and ongoing drama, leading many to believe it would mark the end of Stone Temple Pilots. "In February of 2013, Scott Wyland was kicked out of the Stone Tipple pilots. Too many drugs, too much alcohol, too much drama."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Firing (2013)
xref.body: On February 27, 2013, Stone Temple Pilots "officially terminated Scott Wyland" with a one-line statement, citing his continued drug issues and chronic lateness. Weiland responded by claiming he couldn't be fired as he was a founder of the group. "Stone Temple Pilots have announced that they have officially terminated Scott Wyland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Scott Weiland's Official Termination (February 27, 2013)
xref.body: On February 27, 2013, the band officially terminated Scott Weiland with a one-line statement, following persistent drug issues and his habitual lateness for engagements. Weiland countered by claiming they couldn't fire him from "his band," leading to legal involvement. "On February 27, 2013, he was sacked with this one-line statement. Stone Temple Pilots have announced that they have officially terminated Scott Wyland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Death (December 3, 2015)
xref.body: Scott Weiland was found dead on his tour bus in a hotel parking lot near Minneapolis on December 3, 2015. He was known for his long history of drug and drinking habits and self-destructive behavior, always seemingly on the verge of a fatal incident. "When Scott Wyland was found dead on his tour bus in the parking lot of a hotel, not far from Minneapolis, Wyland was always dancing on the edge of something fatal with his drug and drinking habits and the spurts of self-destructive behavior."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

xref.title: Death on Tour Bus (December 3, 2015)
xref.body: On December 1, 2015, The Wildabouts played in Toronto. On December 2, Weiland went out late with bassist Tommy Black. The next morning, December 3, Weiland woke around 9 AM on the tour bus, then returned to bed as the bus headed to Medina, Minnesota. When the bus arrived in Bloomington, Tommy Black found Weiland unresponsive and stiff around 8 PM after Weiland's wife, Jamie, requested the tour manager, Aaron Moller, check on him due to an unanswered text. Police pronounced him dead at the scene. "At around 8 pm, local time in Minnesota, Moller found Wyland lying in a fetal position on his left side. His eyes were half closed. His body was stiff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Alleged Introduction to Heroin
xref.body: Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers was reportedly the individual who introduced Scott Wyland to heroin. "The first of those junkies was Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers, the guy who apparently introduced Scott to smack in the first place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Artistic Success Compared to Former Bandmates
xref.body: Artistically, Weiland's solo record, 12 Bar Blues, was considered superior to the efforts of his former Stone Temple Pilots bandmates in Talk Show, demonstrating that he possessed a unique quality that made STP special. "Artistically, the winner in this battle was Scott Wyland. I mean, it wasn't even close."

xref.title: Bipolar Disorder
xref.body: A significant factor in Scott Weiland's and Mary Forsberg's struggles was their undiagnosed bipolar disorder, which led to extreme mood swings and poor judgment, often exacerbated by self-medication with drugs like crack. Doctors initially misdiagnosed him with severe depression, and the treatments did not control his manic episodes. "A big part of their problems coping with life is that they were both undiagnosed sufferers of bipolar disorder, and this is a really important part of our story."
